"Modus Operandi" is a Latin phrase. Latin is an ancient language that was once spoken across much of Europe, and many of its words and phrases are still used today in law, science, medicine, and everyday speech.

Breaking it down word by word:

  • Modus = method, mode, or way
  • Operandi = of operating, of working, or of doing

So together, modus operandi means "the way of doing something" — specifically, the particular, habitual method that a person, group, or organization uses to carry out their actions.

It is commonly abbreviated as M.O. (pronounced "em-oh").

Here is the heart of it: everyone has a pattern to the way they do things. A chef always seasons food the same way. A teacher always starts class with a warm-up question. A thief always breaks into the back window instead of the front door.

That pattern — that signature style of doing something — is their modus operandi.

It doesn't just mean what someone does. It means how they consistently do it. The method. The approach. The signature.

Think of it as someone's fingerprint of behavior. Just like a fingerprint is unique to a person, an M.O. is the unique, repeating pattern in the way someone operates.

The term originated in 19th-century law enforcement, particularly in British policing. Detectives noticed that criminals tended to repeat their techniques across different crimes. A forger would always use the same ink. A burglar would always target houses on corner streets. A con artist would always use the same false identity type.

By documenting and studying these patterns, investigators could link multiple crimes to the same person — even without a witness or direct evidence. The phrase modus operandi became the official term for this pattern of criminal behavior, and it spread widely from there.

Over time, the term moved well beyond crime and law enforcement. Today, it is used in three main areas:

1. In Criminal Investigation (Its Original Home)

This is still where the term is most commonly associated. Detectives study a criminal's M.O. to:

  • Connect separate crimes to the same suspect
  • Predict a criminal's next move
  • Build a profile of who they're looking for

For example: "The robber's M.O. was to always strike on rainy nights when surveillance cameras were blurred, always wearing a red jacket, and always targeting ATMs near highway exits for a quick escape."

Every detail of that how — the rain, the jacket, the location choice — forms the M.O.

2. In Business and Organizations

Companies and professionals use "modus operandi" to describe their standard way of working.

For example: "Our M.O. at this startup is to launch fast, collect user feedback, and improve quickly — rather than spending years perfecting a product before releasing it."

Here it simply describes their operating style or philosophy.

3. In Everyday Conversation

People use it casually to describe anyone's habitual way of doing things — not just criminals or companies, but friends, family, or even yourself.

For example:

  • "My brother's M.O. when he's stressed is to go silent for a day, then come back as if nothing happened."
  • "She always arrives 20 minutes early — that's just her M.O."
  • "His M.O. in arguments is to stay very calm and let the other person tire themselves out."
What Makes Something an M.O. (vs. Just a One-Time Action)

This is an important distinction. A modus operandi is not a single action. It is a pattern that repeats. It implies consistency and habit.

If someone lies to you once, that's just a lie. If they consistently deflect blame by bringing up your past mistakes every single time you confront them, that's their M.O. — it's their go-to method, their signature move.

The idea of repetition and consistency is baked into the term. When someone says "that's their M.O.," they're saying: "This isn't random — this is how they always operate."

The grammatically correct plural of modus operandi is modi operandi (from Latin). However, in everyday English, people often just say "modus operandis" informally, and that's widely understood and accepted in casual speech.

Mistake 1: Thinking it only applies to criminals.
It doesn't. Anyone — a teacher, a CEO, a friend, a sports team — can have an M.O. It just means their consistent method of operation.

Mistake 2: Using it for a one-off action.
An M.O. describes a habit or pattern, not something someone did just once.

Mistake 3: Confusing M.O. with motive.
These are related but different. A motive is the reason why someone does something (e.g., greed, revenge). An M.O. is the method of how they do it (e.g., they always hack the system at midnight using a VPN). A detective might say: "The motive was financial gain; the M.O. was phishing emails targeting elderly users."

Modus operandi (M.O.) means the characteristic, repeating method or pattern that someone uses to carry out their actions — whether they're a criminal, a business, or simply a person with a consistent way of doing things.

Once you know this term, you'll start noticing it everywhere — in crime dramas, business meetings, news articles, and daily conversation. And when someone says "that's just their M.O.," you'll know exactly what they mean: that's how they always do it.
